Chapter 8: Facing Loss—Grieving What’s Gone.
Loss is something that never really leaves the side of a child who's been moved from place to place. Every goodbye feels like a tiny heartbreak, a quiet reminder of all that’s been left behind. Imagine having to pack up your life in just a few moments, learning to say goodbye quickly, and trying not to show how much it hurts. But, the pain doesn’t just disappear. It sneaks back in, especially in those quiet moments when everything feels a little too empty.
And then, there’s the loss of his mother. That kind of absence isn’t just a gap; it’s a wound that never truly heals. He remembers her laugh, and the gentle way she’d tuck him in at night. Sometimes, he wonders where she is now. Does she ever think about him? Those questions hang in the air, unanswered. But the longing, the ache—it’s always there.
Of course, those aren’t the only losses. There are friends who slowly drift away, foster siblings who turn into strangers, and houses that blur together until they’re just a long list of places he used to stay. Each of those goodbyes leaves a mark, a little scar that shapes how he sees the world. Most people don’t realize just how much a child can grieve, or how deep that pain can go.
Sometimes, it all gets to be too much. The grief bubbles over, and he lashes out—angry that life can be so unfair. Other times, he just shuts down, pulling away from everyone around him. The adults try to help, but their words often miss the mark. You start to see that there aren’t any easy answers here—no quick fixes for a heart that’s been broken so many times.
But as time goes on, he figures out how to carry his grief, to let it be part of him instead of something he fights against. He leans into small rituals—like writing letters he’ll never send, or visiting places that hold special memories. Sometimes, just holding onto Doggie is enough when the sadness feels too heavy. These little acts don’t erase the pain, but they do make it a bit more bearable.
